newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Democrats strike pension deal with govt.
newsitem.headline: Australian Democrats strike pension deal with govt.

text.p: A tax on Australian pension fund contributions looks set to pass into law after the government brokered a deal with the Australian Democrats minority party to ensure its passage through the upper house of parliament.

A spokesman for the Democrats said the minority party had reached an agreement with the government under which low and middle income earners would be protected from the 15 percent tax on contributions for workers earning more than A$70,000 a year.
Under the deal, members of superannuation funds would receive at least four written warnings that they should provide their tax file numbers to avoid paying the surcharge.
But all new accounts opened with superannuation funds would have to provide tax file numbers or face the surcharge.
Under the agreed amendments, all current members of superannuation funds with annual contributions of less than A$2,000 would also be excluded from the surcharge.
In addition, the Democrats had already succeeded in pushing through an amendment to exempt workers who moved above the A$70,000 a year threshold through retrenchment payouts.

"This achieves the Democrats' objective of ensuring the surcharge won't apply to low income earners, but cannot be avoided by high income earners," Democrats superannuation spokeswoman Lyn Allison said in a statement.
She said the tax file number amendments were certain to pass the non-government dominated Senate when debate resumed on Monday.
But a spokesman for Assistant Treasurer Rod Kemp said there was one Democrat-proposed amendment which the government would not support -- the re-naming of the surcharge as a tax.
"We'll be vehemently opposing that," the spokesman told Reuters. "But apart from that everything seems to be sailing pretty smoothly."
The spokesman said the government would support all of the Democrats' other amendments as the changes were all revenue neutral and also maintained the workability of the legislation.
The government needs two non-government votes to pass any legislation in the Senate.
